segments.text: Chemical thermodynamics asks whether a reaction can happen at all (spontaneity) and how much energy it releases or absorbs, without needing to know how fast it proceeds (that is kinetics, Chapter 4). It uses the same laws met in Physics Chapter IV, applied specifically to chemical systems.

blocks.text: 3. Internal energy, enthalpy, entropy, and Gibbs free energy

segments.text: (H = U + PV) is convenient because, at constant pressure (typical for reactions open to the atmosphere), the enthalpy change equals the heat exchanged — exothermic reactions have negative ΔH, endothermic positive.

(G = H − TS) combines both into a single spontaneity criterion: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. A reaction is spontaneous when ΔG < 0, regardless of whether it is exothermic or endothermic, because a sufficiently large favourable entropy change can drive an endothermic reaction forward (and vice versa).

items.text: State functions (U, H, S, G) depend only on current state, enabling path-independent calculations like Hess’s law.
The first law tracks energy conservation; the second law, via entropy, determines the direction spontaneous processes take.
Gibbs free energy, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, is the single criterion for spontaneity, showing that both enthalpy and entropy changes matter, not enthalpy alone.
ΔG = 0 defines equilibrium and links thermodynamics quantitatively to the equilibrium constant K.
